M16_S01.summary: Twelve types of person are distinguished: four kinds of worldling and the eight noble persons of the four paths and four fruitions.
body: Puggala, from 'puṇ + gala', means a person. A person is a being made up of mentality and materiality — or of mentality alone, or materiality alone — brought into being and governed by the force of kamma.

Twelve types of person are distinguished, in two groups. Group A, the worldlings: 1. the rootless person in a woeful state (Ahetuka puggala); 2. the rootless person in a happy state (Sugati ahetuka puggala); 3. the two-rooted person (Dvihetuka puggala); 4. the three-rooted person (Tihetuka puggala).

Group B, the noble persons: the person of the path and the person of the fruition at each of the four stages — stream-entry (Sotāpatti), once-returning (Sakadāgāmi), non-returning (Anāgāmi) and Arahantship (Arahatta) — 4 paths + 4 fruitions = 8 types.
In conventional truth we speak of persons, human beings, deities and brahmās. In ultimate truth there is only mentality and materiality: no abiding 'person' is to be found.

M16_S02.summary: The rootless person of a woeful state is reborn by the unwholesome-resultant investigating citta, the rootless person of a happy state by the wholesome-resultant one — of whom eleven kinds are listed.
body: The rootless person in a woeful state (Ahetuka puggala) appears in four ways in the course of ordinary life: beings with much suffering and little ease; beings in unmitigated suffering; beings tormented by bodily hunger and thirst; beings worn out by hardship and perpetual fear. For such beings wholesome states of mind are hard to come by.

The rebirth-linking consciousness of such a person is the ROOTLESS UNWHOLESOME-RESULTANT INVESTIGATING CITTA ACCOMPANIED BY EQUANIMITY — the result of 11 unwholesome cittas (8 greed-rooted + 2 hatred-rooted + 1 delusion-rooted associated with doubt). The delusion-rooted citta associated with restlessness cannot produce rebirth, being too scattered and weak; it gives its results only in the course of life.

In the course of life such a person can experience 37 cittas: the 12 unwholesome + 17 rootless cittas (the 18 less the smile-producing citta) + the 8 sense-sphere beautiful wholesome cittas (4 with knowledge and 4 without); and all 52 mental factors.

The rootless person in a happy state (Sugati ahetuka puggala) enjoys far more ease and is spared the torments of the first kind. The rebirth-linking consciousness here is the ROOTLESS WHOLESOME-RESULTANT INVESTIGATING CITTA ACCOMPANIED BY EQUANIMITY, which performs the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death. Such persons are found in the human realm and in the lower ranks of the realm of the Four Great Kings.

There are three modes of birth for them: womb-birth (in the human realm); spontaneous birth (in the realm of the Four Great Kings, appearing at once without passing through a womb); and birth as materiality alone (in the realm of non-percipient beings, where rebirth consists only of matter — the material life faculty, kamma-born materiality and the materiality produced by temperature).

Eleven kinds of rootless person in a happy state are enumerated: those born blind (Jaccandha — born without eye-sensitivity, the eye-sensitivity not having arisen in the first three months in the womb); born deaf; born without nose-sensitivity; born dull-witted; born mute; born mad; the sexless (Paṇḍaka, having neither male nor female organ); the hermaphrodite (Ubhatobyañjanaka); and others of the same kind.

M16_S03.summary: At each of the four stages there is a person of the path and a person of the fruition; the first path destroys three fetters, two mental factors and five cittas, and the fourth uproots all seeds of rebirth.
body: The person of the path of stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga puggala) is one who is in the very act of destroying the three fetters of personality view, doubt and clinging to rites and rituals, realising Nibbāna for the first time. The designation holds exactly for the arising of the path citta, for its three sub-moments of arising, presence and dissolution.

At this first path, two mental factors are destroyed: wrong view and doubt. Five cittas are destroyed: the 4 greed-rooted cittas associated with wrong view (2 with joy and 2 with equanimity) and the delusion-rooted citta associated with doubt.

The person of the fruition of stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala puggala) is one who has attained that path; the stage is also called the first fruit, the fruit of entering the stream. It extends from the first arising of the fruition citta until the moment of dissolution of the purification citta in the process of attaining the second path.

Then follow: the person of the path of once-returning (Sakadāgāmimagga) and the person of its fruition, the second noble stage; and the person of the path of non-returning (Anāgāmimagga) and the person of its fruition.

The person of the path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga puggala) is one who is in the act of UPROOTING every seed of renewed existence; with the person of the fruition of Arahantship, the fourth noble stage, the work is complete.

M16_S04.summary: There are 31 realms in four planes: 4 woeful, 7 happy sense-sphere, 16 form-sphere and 4 formless — and the noble ones are never reborn in the woeful or non-percipient realms.
body: There are four planes of existence (Bhūmi): 1. the woeful plane (Apāyabhūmi); 2. the happy sense-sphere plane (Kāmasugatibhūmi); 3. the form-sphere plane (Rūpāvacarabhūmi); 4. the formless-sphere plane (Arūpāvacarabhūmi).
The woeful plane has four realms: hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts and the realm of asuras.

The happy sense-sphere plane has seven realms: the human realm, the realm of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma deities, the Tusita deities, the deities who delight in creating, and the deities who wield power over others' creations.

The form-sphere plane has 16 realms in four groups according to the level of jhāna: three for the first jhāna (Brahmā's Retinue, Brahmā's Ministers, Great Brahmās); three for the second; three for the third; and seven for the fourth.
The formless plane has four realms: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Remember: once-returners, stream-enterers and worldlings are not reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsā, the five pure realms); and noble persons are never reborn among the non-percipient beings or in any woeful realm.

M16_S05.summary: The woeful plane comprises eight great hells 1,500 leagues apart, each with four gates and sixteen minor hells, together with the animal, ghost and asura realms.
body: The hell realm contains eight great hells: 1. Sañjīva (reviving), 2. Kāḷasutta (black thread), 3. Saṅghāta (crushing), 4. Roruva, 5. Mahāroruva, 6. Tāpana, 7. Mahātāpana, 8. Avīci (unremitting).
They lie deep within the earth, each great hell 1,500 leagues from the next (one league being about 20 km), set one above another in that order.

Each great hell has 4 gates (8 × 4 = 32 gates); each gate has 4 pits (32 × 4 = 128 pits) and a lord of death who governs it (32 in all); and each great hell has 16 minor hells around it, called the hells of much suffering (Ussada).

The animal realm and the realm of ghosts are spread throughout the worlds and have two sides to their existence — just as the realm of the Four Great Kings has a side enjoying heavenly pleasures and a side suffering as in hell.
The asuras (Asura) include the deva-asuras: the asura deities take rebirth by consciousness, as other deities do. They are the lowest rank of deity and have no liking for light.

M16_S06.summary: Human beings are so called from their bright and bold minds; of the four continents, Jambūdīpa is the hardest to live in but the easiest for practice, and it is where Buddhas arise.
body: Kāmasugati, from 'su' (good) and 'gati' (destination), is a happy destination: a plane of pleasure is called a happy sense-sphere realm because it is bound up with sensual craving — craving for forms, sounds, odours, tastes, tangibles and mental objects.

The human realm (Manussabhūmi): 'Manussānaṃ etesanti = Manussā' — beings are called human because their minds are bright and bold. Four classes of human being are distinguished, living in four continents.

1. Jambūdīpa, the southern continent, where we ourselves live (jambū being the rose-apple tree once plentiful in India). The minds of its people differ from those of the other three continents: bright and courageous in good, and fierce and extreme in evil.

This continent is in one sense inferior to the other three, since its people must labour harder and endure more suffering — but for that very reason practice is EASIER here, and it is here that Buddhas arise. On the side of good, one can develop to become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, a chief disciple, a great disciple or an ordinary disciple, a Wheel-turning Monarch, or attain jhāna and the higher knowledges. On the side of evil, the heinous crimes are possible here: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an Arahant, drawing the blood of a Buddha and causing a schism in the Sangha.
2. Uttarakuru, the northern continent; 3. Pubbavideha, the eastern continent (whose people have round faces, matching the round shape of their land); 4. Aparagoyāna, the western continent.

M16_S07.summary: In the six sense-sphere heavens the life span doubles at each level, from 500 celestial years among the Four Great Kings to 16,000 in the realm of Māra at the top.
body: The deities of the six sense-sphere heavens are Uppattideva: deities born there to enjoy the fruit of kamma already made — unlike the brahmās, who are born through the attainment of jhāna.

1. The realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), named after the four kings who govern its hosts. It lies halfway up Mount Sineru, 42,000 leagues from the human world. Its life span is 500 celestial years, one celestial day being 50 human years — some 9,125,000 human years in all. Its deities fall into several groups: earth-bound deities, gandhabbas (who dwell in fragrant trees) and kumbhaṇḍas.

2. The Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa), on the summit of Mount Sineru: the round summit holds the city of Sudassana, built of the seven precious substances, with the Vejayanta palace of Sakka, king of the gods. Its life span is 1,000 celestial years, one day and night being 100 human years. Male deities appear as youths of twenty, female deities as girls of sixteen; there is no ageing, no illness, and their food is pure.
3. The Yāma deities, whose lord is named Suyāma; their realm stands in space. Life span 2,000 celestial years, one day being 200 human years — some 146,000,000 human years.

4. The Tusita deities, the abode of those who live by good conduct with a cool and contented mind. Bodhisattas and future chief disciples dwell here. Life span 4,000 celestial years, one day being 400 human years.

5. The deities who delight in creating (Nimmānarati): life span 8,000 celestial years, one day being 800 human years. 6. The deities who wield power over others' creations (Paranimmitavasavattī): life span 16,000 celestial years, one day being 1,600 human years — and this is the abode of Māra.

The two highest of the six do not have consorts as the four below do (in the realms of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three, the Yāma and the Tusita deities the deities all have consorts): there, when a male or female deity desires, a partner is created by will.

M16_S08.summary: The sixteen form realms are grouped by jhāna, the five Pure Abodes being reserved for non-returners and Arahants, while the four formless realms contain only the four mental aggregates.
body: The form-sphere plane (Rūpāvacarabhūmi) has 16 realms grouped in four sets according to the level of jhāna. They stand in space in three separate regions, built of the seven precious substances and always shining with radiance.

Group one — the three realms of the first jhāna: Brahmā's Retinue (Brahmapārisajjā, the attendants and following of Great Brahmā); Brahmā's Ministers (Brahmapurohitā, the brahmās who serve as counsellors); and the Great Brahmās (Mahābrahmā, the foremost brahmā, the first to appear when a world system forms).

Group two — the three realms of the second jhāna: Minor Lustre, Infinite Lustre and Radiant Lustre (Ābhassarā, whose radiance streams from their bodies; according to the Aggañña Sutta, the ancestors of the human race were brahmās from the Ābhassara realm). Group three — the three realms of the third jhāna: Minor Aura, Infinite Aura and Steady Aura.

Group four — the seven realms of the fourth jhāna: the Very Fruitful (Vehapphala), the non-percipient beings (Asaññasatta, who have materiality only) and the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsā): Avihā, Atappā, Sudassā, Sudassī and Akaniṭṭhā.

The Pure Abodes are the pure dwelling of non-returners and Arahants: a brahmā born there must have attained the fifth form-sphere jhāna and be at least a non-returner. The five are arranged one above another, and Akaniṭṭhā has the highest perfection of virtue, concentration and wisdom in the whole form sphere.

Rebirth in the nine jhāna realms follows the strength of the attainment: the three first-jhāna realms by the force of first-jhāna wholesome kamma, and the three realms of the second and the three of the third jhāna by the force of their corresponding attainments.

The formless plane (Arūpabhūmi) has four realms: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These realms contain only the four mental aggregates — feeling, perception, formations and consciousness — with no aggregate of materiality; the mental aggregates arise and pass away by proximity condition from the rebirth-linking consciousness onward. A formless brahmā is reborn there by the force of jhāna developed through dispassion, through turning away in weariness from materiality.

The life of a brahmā: no male or female characteristics are displayed, though the form resembles that of a man; brahmās delight in their palaces and gardens, yet have no hindrance of sensual desire, since while still human they developed the practice of dispassion; and those who are noble ones enter upon the attainment of fruition.
